(1+ab)2−(a+b)2=1+2ab+a2b2−a2−2ab−b2=1−a2−b2+a2b2  =  (1−a2)(1−b2). \begin{aligned} (1+ab)^{2}-(a+b)^{2} &= 1 + 2ab + a^{2}b^{2} - a^{2} - 2ab - b^{2}\\[3pt] &= 1 - a^{2} - b^{2} + a^{2}b^{2} \;=\; \big(1-a^{2}\big)\big(1-b^{2}\big). \end{aligned} (1+ab)2−(a+b)2​=1+2ab+a2b2−a2−2ab−b2=1−a2−b2+a2b2=(1−a2)(1−b2).​

So

1−β32=1−β12 1−β221+β1β2=1γ1γ2(1+β1β2), \sqrt{1-\beta_{3}^{2}} = \frac{\sqrt{1-\beta_{1}^{2}}\,\sqrt{1-\beta_{2}^{2}}}{1+\beta_{1}\beta_{2}} = \frac{1}{\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}\big(1+\beta_{1}\beta_{2}\big)}, 1−β32​​=1+β1​β2​1−β12​​1−β22​​​=γ1​γ2​(1+β1​β2​)1​,

hence γ3=γ1γ2(1+β1β2)\gamma_{3}=\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}(1+\beta_{1}\beta_{2})γ3​=γ1​γ2​(1+β1​β2​), which is the prefactor. ✓

Keep that identity. (1+ab)2−(a+b)2=(1−a2)(1−b2)(1+ab)^{2}-(a+b)^{2}=(1-a^{2})(1-b^{2})(1+ab)2−(a+b)2=(1−a2)(1−b2) — and its sibling (1−ab)2−(a−b)2=(1−a2)(1−b2)(1-ab)^{2}-(a-b)^{2}=(1-a^{2})(1-b^{2})(1−ab)2−(a−b)2=(1−a2)(1−b2) — will do the work again in §5 (proving you cannot reach ccc by combining sub-ccc speeds) and once more in §6, where it will turn out to be the hyperbolic addition formula in disguise. Three appearances of one factorisation is usually a sign that something structural is going on, and it is.

The other group axioms. Λ(0)=I\Lambda(0)=IΛ(0)=I is the identity. Λ(−β)\Lambda(-\beta)Λ(−β) is the inverse, since (2.2.26) with β2=−β1\beta_{2}=-\beta_{1}β2​=−β1​ gives β3=0\beta_{3}=0β3​=0. Associativity is free — matrix multiplication is associative. So the boosts along a fixed axis form a one-parameter group, and §6 finds the parameter that makes it look like one.

This matters more than it looks. Closure is not automatic: it is a statement that the set of transformations is a self-consistent family, that "the frames of physics" is a coherent notion, and that no chain of boosts can ever take you outside the theory. Had the composition of two boosts failed to be a boost, the whole scheme would have been incoherent.

But look hard at (2.2.26). The composed parameter is not β1+β2\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}β1​+β2​. Boost by 0.5c0.5c0.5c and then by 0.5c0.5c0.5c again and you get

β3=0.5+0.51+0.25=11.25=0.8, \beta_{3} = \frac{0.5+0.5}{1+0.25} = \frac{1}{1.25} = 0.8, β3​=1+0.250.5+0.5​=1.251​=0.8, (2.2.28)

not 111. Two half-light-speed boosts give eight tenths, and no finite chain of sub-ccc boosts will ever reach ccc — which §5 proves properly and §6 explains. Velocity is the wrong variable to be adding.

⚠ One caveat, flagged now and paid in Problem 3

Everything above was for boosts along one fixed axis. Boosts along different axes do not compose into a pure boost: the product picks up a spatial rotation, the Wigner rotation. Problem 3 derives that the effect must exist, in two lines, from the fact that (2.2.24) is a symmetric matrix. The physical consequence — Thomas precession — is a measurable contribution to atomic fine structure, and it is a genuinely relativistic effect with no Newtonian ancestor at all.

In plain terms 2.2.3

Whether a family of transformations closes on itself decides whether you have a theory or a formula. Compose two boosts along one axis and the result is another boost, with a parameter emphatically not the sum of the two, since half the speed of light followed by half the speed of light delivers eight tenths. Closure is neither automatic nor decorative, because had it failed there would be no coherent notion of the frames of physics, and some chain of changes of viewpoint would have carried you outside the theory.

Two smaller facts fall out along the way. The transformation has determinant one, so it preserves four-dimensional volume, which is the determinant doing the job the toolkit gave it. And the whole apparatus is now a matrix acting on four numbers, so composing changes of frame has become multiplying matrices and nothing more.

One caveat is worth flagging because it has no ancestor in older physics. Boosts along a single axis behave; boosts along different axes do not compose into a boost at all, and the product leaves a spatial rotation behind. That rotation is measurable, contributing to the fine structure of atomic spectra, and nothing in Newtonian mechanics predicts anything of the kind. The composition rule also says plainly that velocity is the wrong quantity to be adding.

4 · The three consequences

Now we cash it in. Three results, and every one of them is a two-line substitution into (2.2.19). The difficulty in this material is never the algebra; it is knowing which two events you are transforming. So each subsection begins by stating the operational question — who measures what, with which apparatus, and using which pair of events — before any symbol moves.

4.1 · Relativity of simultaneity

The operational question. Two firecrackers explode. An observer in SSS, using clocks that have been synchronised throughout SSS, records both explosions at the same reading. What do the clocks of S′S'S′ — synchronised throughout S′S'S′ — record?

Take two events with Δt=0\Delta t=0Δt=0 and Δx≠0\Delta x\neq0Δx=0 in SSS. From (2.2.19), applied to the separation (legitimate because the transformation is linear, which is what §1 bought us):

c Δt′=γ(c Δt−β Δx)=−γβ Δx⟹Δt′=−γβ Δxc  ≠  0. c\,\Delta t' = \gamma\big(c\,\Delta t - \beta\,\Delta x\big) = -\gamma\beta\,\Delta x \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \Delta t' = -\frac{\gamma\beta\,\Delta x}{c} \;\neq\; 0. cΔt′=γ(cΔt−βΔx)=−γβΔx⟹Δt′=−cγβΔx​=0. (2.2.29)

Events simultaneous in SSS are not simultaneous in S′S'S′, unless they happen at the same place. The sign matters and is worth reading off: if Δx>0\Delta x \gt 0Δx>0 — the second event is further along the direction of S′S'S′'s motion — then Δt′<0\Delta t' \lt 0Δt′<0, so in S′S'S′ the leading event happened first. The frame that is moving forward sees the forward event as earlier.

A concrete case

A train of proper length 300 m300\ \mathrm{m}300 m passes a platform at β=0.6\beta=0.6β=0.6, so γ=1.25\gamma=1.25γ=1.25. Lightning strikes both ends of the train — simultaneously, as judged on the platform.

In the platform frame SSS the train is contracted (§4.3) to 300/1.25=240 m300/1.25=240\ \mathrm{m}300/1.25=240 m, so the two strike events have Δx=240 m\Delta x=240\ \mathrm{m}Δx=240 m, Δt=0\Delta t=0Δt=0. On the train,

Δt′=−γβΔxc=−1.25×0.6×2402.998×108 s=−6.00×10−7 s=−600 ns, \Delta t' = -\frac{\gamma\beta\Delta x}{c} = -\frac{1.25\times0.6\times240}{2.998\times10^{8}}\ \mathrm{s} = -6.00\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{s} = -600\ \mathrm{ns}, Δt′=−cγβΔx​=−2.998×1081.25×0.6×240​ s=−6.00×10−7 s=−600 ns, (2.2.30)

and Δx′=γΔx=1.25×240=300 m\Delta x' = \gamma\Delta x = 1.25\times240 = 300\ \mathrm{m}Δx′=γΔx=1.25×240=300 m ✓ — the train's own length, as it must be. So on the train, the front is struck 600 ns600\ \mathrm{ns}600 ns before the rear. Not "appears to be": is, in every sense that the train's own clocks can express.

Check it without the transformation, as a sanity test. Both flashes travel at ccc in the platform frame and meet at the midpoint of the two strike locations. Meanwhile the train's midpoint is moving toward the front strike, so it runs into the front flash first. Now argue in the train frame: the train observer sits midway between the two scorch marks on the train, both flashes travel to them at ccc over equal distances, and the front flash arrives first. Equal distances, equal speeds, different arrival times — therefore different emission times. The front strike happened first. Two independent routes, one answer. ✓

Why this one goes first

Time dilation and length contraction are not independent phenomena sitting alongside the failure of simultaneity. They are consequences of it. Every apparent paradox in the rest of this chapter — and in the rest of the subject — is resolved by finding the place where somebody assumed two distant events had a frame-independent time order.

Readers who meet dilation and contraction first almost never recover, because they acquire a picture in which clocks and rulers are mysteriously defective while "now" remains universal. It does not. There is no universal "now". There is a family of them, one per state of motion, and they cut through spacetime at different angles. Hold that and nothing that follows can confuse you.

4.2 · Time dilation

The operational question. A single clock rides along with S′S'S′ and ticks twice. The elapsed time it reads between the ticks is Δτ\Delta\tauΔτ — this is called the clock's proper time, and it is what that particular clock actually displays. What is the elapsed time between those same two ticks according to SSS, where the reading must be taken off two different synchronised clocks, one at each tick's location?

The clock is at rest in S′S'S′, so the two ticks have Δx′=0\Delta x'=0Δx′=0 and Δt′=Δτ\Delta t'=\Delta\tauΔt′=Δτ. We want Δt\Delta tΔt, so use the inverse transformation from the grind box in §2.3:

c Δt=γ(c Δt′+β Δx′)=γ c Δτ⟹  Δt=γ Δτ   c\,\Delta t = \gamma\big(c\,\Delta t' + \beta\,\Delta x'\big) = \gamma\,c\,\Delta\tau \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \boxed{\;\Delta t = \gamma\,\Delta\tau\;} cΔt=γ(cΔt′+βΔx′)=γcΔτ⟹Δt=γΔτ​ (2.2.31)

Since γ≥1\gamma\geq1γ≥1, more time elapses in SSS than the moving clock records. A moving clock runs slow, by exactly γ\gammaγ. Note the asymmetry in the apparatus, which is where all the content is: one clock on one side, two clocks on the other.

The symmetric version, and why it is not a contradiction

Run the identical argument the other way. A clock at rest in SSS ticks twice, Δx=0\Delta x=0Δx=0, Δt=ΔτS\Delta t=\Delta\tau_{S}Δt=ΔτS​. Then (2.2.19) gives directly cΔt′=γ(cΔτS−0)c\Delta t'=\gamma(c\Delta\tau_{S}-0)cΔt′=γ(cΔτS​−0), so Δt′=γΔτS\Delta t'=\gamma\Delta\tau_{S}Δt′=γΔτS​. Each observer finds the other's clock slow, by the same factor. Both statements are true. Both are derived from the same transformation. There is no contradiction, and here is the accounting that shows it.

Set β=0.6\beta=0.6β=0.6, γ=1.25\gamma=1.25γ=1.25. In SSS there are two clocks, C1C_{1}C1​ at x=0x=0x=0 and C2C_{2}C2​ at x=12x=12x=12 light-seconds, synchronised in SSS. A traveller carrying clock C′C'C′ flies from C1C_{1}C1​ to C2C_{2}C2​.

Told by SSS: the trip takes Δt=12/0.6=20 s\Delta t = 12/0.6 = 20\ \mathrm{s}Δt=12/0.6=20 s. The traveller's clock, moving, runs slow, and reads 20/1.25=16 s20/1.25 = 16\ \mathrm{s}20/1.25=16 s on arrival. C2C_{2}C2​ reads 20 s20\ \mathrm{s}20 s.

Told by S′S'S′: the traveller is at rest and the whole SSS apparatus streams past at 0.6c0.6c0.6c. The distance from C1C_{1}C1​ to C2C_{2}C2​ is contracted to 12/1.25=9.612/1.25=9.612/1.25=9.6 light-seconds, so it takes 9.6/0.6=16 s9.6/0.6 = 16\ \mathrm{s}9.6/0.6=16 s — matching the traveller's own clock, since it is his own clock. During those 161616 seconds the SSS clocks, being the moving ones now, tick only 16/1.25=12.8 s16/1.25 = 12.8\ \mathrm{s}16/1.25=12.8 s.

Contradiction? C2C_{2}C2​ must read 20 s20\ \mathrm{s}20 s when the traveller arrives — that is a local coincidence, two objects at the same place, and no one can disagree about it. Yet S′S'S′ says the SSS clocks advanced only 12.8 s12.8\ \mathrm{s}12.8 s. The missing 7.2 s7.2\ \mathrm{s}7.2 s is exactly the simultaneity offset. At the moment the traveller passes C1C_{1}C1​ (call it t′=0t'=0t′=0), the SSS clocks that S′S'S′ regards as simultaneous satisfy t=βx/ct = \beta x/ct=βx/c, so C2C_{2}C2​ — sitting at x=12x=12x=12 light-seconds — already reads

tC2=βxc=0.6×12=7.2 s. t_{C_{2}} = \frac{\beta x}{c} = 0.6\times 12 = 7.2\ \mathrm{s}. tC2​​=cβx​=0.6×12=7.2 s. (2.2.32)

In the traveller's reckoning, C2C_{2}C2​ was never synchronised with C1C_{1}C1​ in the first place: it was 7.2 s7.2\ \mathrm{s}7.2 s ahead before the trip began. So the books balance:

7.2⏟head start  +  12.8⏟ticked during the trip  =  20.0⏟what C2 reads✓ \underbrace{7.2}_{\text{head start}} \;+\; \underbrace{12.8}_{\text{ticked during the trip}} \;=\; \underbrace{20.0}_{\text{what }C_{2}\text{ reads}} \quad\checkmark head start7.2​​+ticked during the trip12.8​​=what C2​ reads20.0​​✓ (2.2.33)

Both frames agree on every local coincidence — which clock reads what when it is next to which other clock. They disagree only about the synchronisation of distant clocks, which is not an observable but a convention imposed frame by frame. The symmetry of time dilation is consistent precisely because simultaneity fails, and the failure is exactly the right size. It could not have been any other size: (2.2.29) and (2.2.31) came out of the same matrix.

⚠ Why this isn't obvious

"Each sees the other's clock run slow" sounds like a<ba \lt ba<b and b<ab \lt ab<a. It is not, because the two statements are not comparisons of the same things. Each is a comparison of one clock against a pair of clocks synchronised in the other frame — and the two frames use different pairs, synchronised differently. Strip out the words and write down which events are being compared, and the appearance of contradiction evaporates every single time.

Here is the test to apply whenever you feel the vertigo: ask whether the disputed claim is about a local coincidence. "Clock C′C'C′ reads 161616 while sitting next to C2C_{2}C2​, which reads 202020" is a coincidence — two objects, one place, one event — and every frame agrees on it. "Clock C′C'C′ reads 161616 while C2C_{2}C2​, twelve light-seconds away, reads 202020" is not; it invokes a simultaneity convention, and frames are entitled to differ. All the paradoxes are manufactured by smuggling the second kind of statement in wearing the clothes of the first.

4.3 · Length contraction

The operational question, and it is the whole difficulty. A rod lies at rest in S′S'S′ along the x′x'x′-axis. Its ends are at xL′x'_{L}xL′​ and xR′x'_{R}xR′​, always, so its length in S′S'S′ is unambiguous: L0=xR′−xL′L_{0}=x'_{R}-x'_{L}L0​=xR′​−xL′​, called the proper length. Now ask SSS for the rod's length. In SSS the rod is moving, so "where its ends are" is a function of time, and to get a length you must locate both ends at the same moment. At the same moment according to whom? To SSS — that is what it means for SSS to measure a length.

So a length measurement is a pair of events (locate left end, locate right end) constrained by Δt=0\Delta t=0Δt=0 in the measuring frame. The moment you write that down, the answer is forced, because the constraint is a simultaneity constraint and §4.1 already told you those are frame-dependent.

Apply (2.2.19) to the pair. In SSS: Δx=L\Delta x = LΔx=L (what we want) and Δt=0\Delta t=0Δt=0 (the definition of measuring). In S′S'S′: Δx′=L0\Delta x' = L_{0}Δx′=L0​, since the rod is at rest there and it does not matter when you look. Then

Δx′=γ(Δx−β c Δt)=γ Δx⟹L0=γL, \Delta x' = \gamma\big(\Delta x - \beta\,c\,\Delta t\big) = \gamma\,\Delta x \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad L_{0} = \gamma L, Δx′=γ(Δx−βcΔt)=γΔx⟹L0​=γL, (2.2.34)
  L=L0γ=L01−β2  ≤  L0.   \boxed{\;L = \frac{L_{0}}{\gamma} = L_{0}\sqrt{1-\beta^{2}} \;\leq\; L_{0}.\;} L=γL0​​=L0​1−β2​≤L0​.​ (2.2.35)

A moving rod is short, by γ\gammaγ, along its direction of motion only (y′=yy'=yy′=y, z′=zz'=zz′=z means nothing happens across it). And Chapter 2.1's loose end is tied: this is precisely the 1−β2\sqrt{1-\beta^{2}}1−β2​ that FitzGerald and Lorentz had to postulate to explain Michelson–Morley. Here it is a theorem.

It follows from simultaneity — watch

The derivation used Δt=0\Delta t=0Δt=0, which by (2.2.29) means the two measurement events are not simultaneous in S′S'S′:

Δt′=−γβ Δxc=−γβLc=−βL0c. \Delta t' = -\frac{\gamma\beta\,\Delta x}{c} = -\frac{\gamma\beta L}{c} = -\frac{\beta L_{0}}{c}. Δt′=−cγβΔx​=−cγβL​=−cβL0​​. (2.2.36)

From the rod's own frame, SSS located the right end first and the left end βL0/c\beta L_{0}/cβL0​/c later. Since the rod is not going anywhere in S′S'S′, that sloppiness costs SSS nothing — the ends are where they always are — which is why SSS still gets a definite answer. But it is exactly why the answer is not L0L_{0}L0​. To see that the choice of event pair is doing all the work, redo the calculation with a pair that is simultaneous in S′S'S′ instead:

Δt′=0  ⟹  c Δt=β Δx⟹  Δx′=γ(Δx−β2 Δx)=Δxγ  ⟹  Δx=γ Δx′. \begin{aligned} \Delta t' = 0 \;&\Longrightarrow\; c\,\Delta t = \beta\,\Delta x\\[4pt] &\Longrightarrow\; \Delta x' = \gamma\big(\Delta x - \beta^{2}\,\Delta x\big) = \frac{\Delta x}{\gamma} \;\Longrightarrow\; \Delta x = \gamma\,\Delta x'. \end{aligned} Δt′=0​⟹cΔt=βΔx⟹Δx′=γ(Δx−β2Δx)=γΔx​⟹Δx=γΔx′.​ (2.2.37)

Same rod, same frames, different pair of events, and the answer flips from L0/γL_{0}/\gammaL0​/γ to γL0\gamma L_{0}γL0​. The contraction is not a property of the rod. It is a property of the measurement, and specifically of whose simultaneity slices the measurement uses. Nothing was squeezed. Two observers sliced the same four-dimensional object at different angles and got different cross-sections, exactly as two people slicing the same sausage at different angles get ellipses of different lengths. Chapter 2.3 makes that picture precise; here the algebra already contains it.

⚠ Why this isn't obvious — contraction is not "looking squashed"

Length contraction is a statement about a simultaneous measurement. It is not a statement about what a camera records, and the two differ, because light from different parts of an object takes different times to reach the lens. A photograph does not capture a simultaneity slice; it captures the events whose light arrives together.

Work out the difference for a cube of side LLL flying past at β\betaβ, seen from far away, edge-on. Light from the rear face must set out earlier than light from the front face — earlier by L/cL/cL/c, the extra distance — in order to arrive at the camera together. During that L/cL/cL/c the cube moves a distance βL\beta LβL, so the rear face is displaced sideways in the image by βL\beta LβL; you can see round the back of the cube. Meanwhile the front face, measured simultaneously, is contracted to L1−β2L\sqrt{1-\beta^{2}}L1−β2​. Now compare with a cube that is not moving at all but has been rotated by an angle θ\thetaθ: its front face projects to Lcos⁡θL\cos\thetaLcosθ and one side face becomes visible with projected width Lsin⁡θL\sin\thetaLsinθ. Match them:

sin⁡θ=β,cos⁡θ=1−β2✓ \sin\theta = \beta, \qquad \cos\theta = \sqrt{1-\beta^{2}} \quad\checkmark sinθ=β,cosθ=1−β2​✓

The photograph of a rapidly moving cube is the photograph of a rotated cube, turned by θ=arcsin⁡β\theta=\arcsin\betaθ=arcsinβ. ⚑ The general theorem — that a small object of any shape appears rotated rather than contracted, and that a sphere always photographs as a perfectly circular disc — is the Terrell–Penrose result of 1959; the cube calculation above is the whole idea, and the general case is bookkeeping over solid angle.

So: contraction is real and it is not visual. If someone shows you a picture of a squashed spaceship, the picture is wrong. The spaceship is shorter, measured; it does not look shorter, photographed.

Familiar ground — time dilation is an accelerated failure time model

Muon decay is first-order. A population at rest obeys the survival function S0(τ)=e−τ/τ0S_{0}(\tau)=\ee^{-\tau/\tau_{0}}S0​(τ)=e−τ/τ0​ with τ0=2.197 μs\tau_{0}=2.197\ \mathrm{\mu s}τ0​=2.197 μs, which is Chapter 0.1's clearance curve with a different label on the constant. Nothing in (2.2.31) touches that law. What it touches is the argument fed into it.

Watched from the ground, a beam of muons moving at βc\beta cβc has survival

S(t)  =  S0 ⁣(tγ)  =  exp⁡ ⁣(−tγτ0), S(t) \;=\; S_{0}\!\left(\frac{t}{\gamma}\right) \;=\; \exp\!\left(-\frac{t}{\gamma\tau_{0}}\right), S(t)=S0​(γt​)=exp(−γτ0​t​),

and a survival function of the form S(t)=S0(t/φ)S(t)=S_{0}(t/\varphi)S(t)=S0​(t/φ) is, by definition, an accelerated failure time model with acceleration factor φ\varphiφ. Special relativity is an AFT model whose covariate is speed and whose factor is φ=γ\varphi=\gammaφ=γ. That is not a resemblance, it is the same equation, and the reason relativity picks AFT rather than proportional hazards is the physical content of this whole chapter. Proportional hazards would say that motion alters the muon's internal decay rate, which is a claim about muons. AFT says the muon's clock has been rescaled and the decay rate per tick of that clock is untouched, which is a claim about geometry — and therefore one that every particle obeys identically, whatever it is made of.

For an exponential the two models coincide, since scaling the time axis and scaling the hazard are the same operation there. That is exactly why the cosmic-ray calculation of §8 is easy, and exactly why it is easy to take the wrong moral from it. Had the muon decayed with a Weibull hazard the two readings would have parted company, and only the AFT one would have survived the experiment.

What breaks. φ\varphiφ is not fitted. It is γ=(1−β2)−1/2\gamma=(1-\beta^{2})^{-1/2}γ=(1−β2)−1/2, forced by §2 with no free parameter and no residual heterogeneity whatever: two muons at the same speed have exactly the same acceleration factor, so there is no frailty term and nothing left over to model. And the covariate is not a property of the subject at all but of the observer, which is why §8's second telling — done in the muon's own frame, where φ=1\varphi=1φ=1 and the atmosphere is contracted instead — returns the identical count of survivors at the detector. It has to. Whether a given muon reaches the ground is one event, and the two frames are describing it, not deciding it.

In plain terms 2.2.4

Three consequences come out of one substitution, and the order in which they are met decides whether the subject ever becomes intelligible. The root fact is that two events at the same time but different places for one observer are not at the same time for another, and the two famous effects follow from it rather than accompany it. Readers who meet them the other way round acquire a picture in which clocks and rulers are mysteriously defective while the word now stays universal, and they rarely recover.

It does not stay universal. Each state of motion carries its own family of nows, cutting through spacetime at different angles, which is what the local conservation laws of the last part were built to survive. It is also why each observer finding the other's clock slow is no contradiction: one clock is compared against a pair synchronised in the other frame, the two observers use different pairs, and the offset between them is exactly the size that balances the books.

Contraction turns out to be a property of the measurement rather than of the rod. Locating both ends at one moment is a demand about simultaneity, so different observers use different pairs of events and get different answers, and a pair the rod's own frame calls simultaneous flips the answer the other way. Nothing was squeezed, and nothing was done to the rod.

5 · Velocity addition

An object moves at velocity uuu along xxx in frame SSS. What velocity u′u'u′ does S′S'S′ assign it? Galileo says u′=u−vu'=u-vu′=u−v — the velocity-composition rule of Chapter 2.1 §1.2 — and it is exactly what Postulate 2 refuses to accept for light. So derive the replacement.

Velocity is a ratio of displacements, so take differentials of (2.2.19) — legitimate because the coefficients are constants, so the differentials obey the same linear relations as the coordinates:

dx′=γ(dx−v dt),dt′=γ(dt−v dxc2). \dd x' = \gamma\big(\dd x - v\,\dd t\big), \qquad \dd t' = \gamma\left(\dd t - \frac{v\,\dd x}{c^{2}}\right). dx′=γ(dx−vdt),dt′=γ(dt−c2vdx​). (2.2.38)

Divide. The factors of γ\gammaγ cancel — a small mercy, and a hint that the result depends on β\betaβ less violently than one might fear:

u′=dx′dt′=dx−v dtdt−v dx/c2=dxdt−v1−vc2dxdt, u' = \frac{\dd x'}{\dd t'} = \frac{\dd x - v\,\dd t}{\dd t - v\,\dd x/c^{2}} = \frac{\dfrac{\dd x}{\dd t} - v}{1 - \dfrac{v}{c^{2}}\dfrac{\dd x}{\dd t}}, u′=dt′dx′​=dt−vdx/c2dx−vdt​=1−c2v​dtdx​dtdx​−v​, (2.2.39)
  u′=u−v1−uvc2  equivalentlyβu′=βu−βv1−βuβv. \boxed{\; u' = \frac{u-v}{1 - \dfrac{uv}{c^{2}}} \;} \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \beta_{u'} = \frac{\beta_{u}-\beta_{v}}{1-\beta_{u}\beta_{v}}. u′=1−c2uv​u−v​​equivalentlyβu′​=1−βu​βv​βu​−βv​​. (2.2.40)

The dimensionless form is (2.2.26) with a sign flipped, as it should be: composing two boosts and transforming a velocity are the same operation seen from two sides.

5.1 · The postulate reproduces itself

Set u=cu=cu=c and turn the crank:

u′=c−v1−cvc2=c−v1−vc=c (c−v)c−v=c. u' = \frac{c-v}{1-\dfrac{cv}{c^{2}}} = \frac{c-v}{1-\dfrac{v}{c}} = \frac{c\,(c-v)}{c-v} = c. u′=1−c2cv​c−v​=1−cv​c−v​=c−vc(c−v)​=c. (2.2.41)

For any vvv with ∣v∣<c\abs{v}\lt c∣v∣<c. This is a real check, not a tautology dressed up. We imposed the invariance of ccc only for a pulse emitted from the origin at t=0t=0t=0 along ±x\pm x±x; the transformation that resulted now certifies that any object moving at ccc in SSS moves at ccc in every frame — anywhere, any time, either direction. A theory that failed this would have been inconsistent with its own founding assumption.

5.2 · You cannot get to ccc by adding speeds

Claim. If ∣βu∣<1\abs{\beta_{u}}\lt1∣βu​∣<1 and ∣βv∣<1\abs{\beta_{v}}\lt1∣βv​∣<1 then ∣βu′∣<1\abs{\beta_{u'}}\lt1∣βu′​∣<1.

Proof. First, the denominator never vanishes: ∣βuβv∣<1\abs{\beta_{u}\beta_{v}}\lt1∣βu​βv​∣<1, so 1−βuβv>01-\beta_{u}\beta_{v}\gt01−βu​βv​>0. Now compute, using the identity from the §3 grind box in its second form, (1−ab)2−(a−b)2=(1−a2)(1−b2)(1-ab)^{2}-(a-b)^{2}=(1-a^{2})(1-b^{2})(1−ab)2−(a−b)2=(1−a2)(1−b2):

1−βu′2=(1−βuβv)2−(βu−βv)2(1−βuβv)2=(1−βu2)(1−βv2)(1−βuβv)2. 1-\beta_{u'}^{2} = \frac{\big(1-\beta_{u}\beta_{v}\big)^{2}-\big(\beta_{u}-\beta_{v}\big)^{2}}{\big(1-\beta_{u}\beta_{v}\big)^{2}} = \frac{\big(1-\beta_{u}^{2}\big)\big(1-\beta_{v}^{2}\big)}{\big(1-\beta_{u}\beta_{v}\big)^{2}}. 1−βu′2​=(1−βu​βv​)2(1−βu​βv​)2−(βu​−βv​)2​=(1−βu​βv​)2(1−βu2​)(1−βv2​)​. (2.2.42)

Every factor on the right is strictly positive, so 1−βu′2>01-\beta_{u'}^{2}\gt01−βu′2​>0, so ∣βu′∣<1\abs{\beta_{u'}}\lt1∣βu′​∣<1. ■\blacksquare■

Read (2.2.42) once more, because it says more than the claim. It says the "distance from ccc", measured by 1−β21-\beta^{2}1−β2, is multiplicative under composition: combine two sub-light speeds and the product of their deficits is what survives. You can multiply small positive numbers together forever and never reach zero. The light barrier is not a wall someone installed; it is the statement that a product of positives is positive.

5.3 · And at ordinary speeds, Galileo

For uv/c2≪1uv/c^{2}\ll1uv/c2≪1, expand the denominator (Chapter 0.3):

u′=(u−v)(1+uvc2+⋯ )=u−v+uv(u−v)c2+⋯ u' = (u-v)\left(1+\frac{uv}{c^{2}}+\cdots\right) = u - v + \frac{uv(u-v)}{c^{2}} + \cdots u′=(u−v)(1+c2uv​+⋯)=u−v+c2uv(u−v)​+⋯ (2.2.43)

Two cars approaching each other at 30 m s−130\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}30 ms−1 each (u=+30u=+30u=+30, v=−30v=-30v=−30): the Galilean answer is 60 m s−160\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}60 ms−1 and the correction is

uv(u−v)c2=(30)(−30)(60)8.99×1016=−6.0×10−13 m s−1, \frac{uv(u-v)}{c^{2}} = \frac{(30)(-30)(60)}{8.99\times10^{16}} = -6.0\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}, c2uv(u−v)​=8.99×1016(30)(−30)(60)​=−6.0×10−13 ms−1, (2.2.44)

a relative error of one part in 101410^{14}1014. This is why the Galilean rule survived so long unchallenged: on a motorway it is wrong in the fourteenth decimal place.

⚠ Why this isn't obvious — some speeds may exceed ccc, and it is fine

Nothing above forbids coordinate speeds greater than ccc. What is forbidden is the transport of matter, energy or information faster than ccc. Two examples, both computed.

A spotlight on a distant wall. Rotate a laser at angular rate ω\omegaω; the spot on a wall at distance RRR moves at vspot=ωRv_{\text{spot}}=\omega Rvspot​=ωR, with no upper bound. Point a laser at the Moon (R=3.84×108 mR=3.84\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m}R=3.84×108 m) and spin it at one revolution per second, ω=2π s−1\omega=2\pi\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}ω=2π s−1:

vspot=2π×3.84×108=2.41×109 m s−1=8.05 c. v_{\text{spot}} = 2\pi\times3.84\times10^{8} = 2.41\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} = 8.05\,c. vspot​=2π×3.84×108=2.41×109 ms−1=8.05c.

No rule is broken, because the spot is not a thing. The photons landing at one place and the photons landing at the next place travelled independently from the laser; nothing went sideways. You cannot send a message along the wall this way — each point of the wall learns only about the laser, never about its neighbours.

A pair of scissors. Two straight edges crossing at a small angle θ\thetaθ, one sliding toward the other at speed vvv. The moving edge is y=xtan⁡θ+vty = x\tan\theta + vty=xtanθ+vt, so the intersection with y=0y=0y=0 sits at x=−vt/tan⁡θx = -vt/\tan\thetax=−vt/tanθ and travels at v/tan⁡θv/\tan\thetav/tanθ — unbounded as θ→0\theta\to0θ→0. With v=100 m s−1v=100\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}v=100 ms−1 and θ=10−7 rad\theta = 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{rad}θ=10−7 rad the crossing point moves at 3.3 c3.3\,c3.3c. Again nothing is transported; the intersection is a geometric coincidence, not an object, and a real pair of scissors would in any case not be rigid — closing the handles sends a wave down the blade at the speed of sound in steel.

The rule to carry: ask what is being transported. If the answer is "nothing", any speed is allowed.

In plain terms 2.2.5

The rule replacing the addition of velocities earns its place by passing a test nobody arranged for it. Invariance of the light speed was imposed for one pulse leaving one origin in one of two directions, and the rule that resulted now certifies that anything travelling at that speed in one frame travels at it in every frame, anywhere, at any time, in any direction.

The barrier that follows is not a wall anybody installed. Rate a speed by the quantity measuring its distance from the limit, and combining two speeds multiplies the two ratings together, up to a positive factor. Small positive numbers can be multiplied together forever without reaching zero, so no finite chain of ordinary boosts arrives at the limit, and the whole of the light barrier is the observation that a product of positive numbers is positive.

None of this forbids coordinate speeds above the limit, and it is worth being clear which is which. Sweep a laser across the face of the Moon and the spot crosses it many times faster than light, because the photons landing at one place and those landing next door travelled independently and nothing went sideways. Close a pair of shears at a shallow enough angle and the crossing point outruns light for the same reason. Ask what is being transported, and where the answer is nothing, any speed is permitted.

6 · Rapidity — the parameter that behaves

Velocities do not add. Something must, because §3 showed that boosts along an axis form a one-parameter group, and a one-parameter group has an additive parameter almost by definition: composing two elements should add their labels, the way rotating by 30∘30^{\circ}30∘ and then 40∘40^{\circ}40∘ gives 70∘70^{\circ}70∘. We simply chose a bad label. Find the good one.

The composition rule (2.2.26),

β3=β1+β21+β1β2, \beta_{3} = \frac{\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}}{1+\beta_{1}\beta_{2}}, β3​=1+β1​β2​β1​+β2​​, (2.2.45)

is not a formula anyone would invent — but it is a formula everyone has seen. It is the addition theorem for the hyperbolic tangent. So define the rapidity ϕ\phiϕ by

β  =  tanh⁡ϕ,equivalentlyϕ=artanh⁡β=12ln⁡ ⁣1+β1−β. \beta \;=\; \tanh\phi, \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \phi = \operatorname{artanh}\beta = \tfrac12\ln\!\frac{1+\beta}{1-\beta}. β=tanhϕ,equivalentlyϕ=artanhβ=21​ln1−β1+β​. (2.2.46)

This is a legitimate change of variable: tanh⁡\tanhtanh maps R\RR one-to-one onto (−1,1)(-1,1)(−1,1), exactly the allowed range of β\betaβ, and it is smooth with a smooth inverse. Every subluminal velocity has exactly one rapidity, and every real number is somebody's rapidity.

6.1 · What γ\gammaγ becomes

Divide the identity cosh⁡2ϕ−sinh⁡2ϕ=1\cosh^{2}\phi-\sinh^{2}\phi=1cosh2ϕ−sinh2ϕ=1 by cosh⁡2ϕ\cosh^{2}\phicosh2ϕ to get 1−tanh⁡2ϕ=1/cosh⁡2ϕ1-\tanh^{2}\phi=1/\cosh^{2}\phi1−tanh2ϕ=1/cosh2ϕ. Hence

γ=11−β2=11−tanh⁡2ϕ=cosh⁡ϕ,γβ=cosh⁡ϕtanh⁡ϕ=sinh⁡ϕ. \gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\beta^{2}}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\tanh^{2}\phi}} = \cosh\phi, \qquad \gamma\beta = \cosh\phi\tanh\phi = \sinh\phi. γ=1−β2​1​=1−tanh2ϕ​1​=coshϕ,γβ=coshϕtanhϕ=sinhϕ. (2.2.47)

Substituting into (2.2.24), the boost is

(ct′x′)=(cosh⁡ϕ−sinh⁡ϕ−sinh⁡ϕcosh⁡ϕ)(ctx), \begin{pmatrix} ct'\\ x'\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \cosh\phi & -\sinh\phi\\ -\sinh\phi & \cosh\phi\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} ct\\ x\end{pmatrix}, (ct′x′​)=(coshϕ−sinhϕ​−sinhϕcoshϕ​)(ctx​), (2.2.48)

and the transformation reads ct′=ctcosh⁡ϕ−xsinh⁡ϕct'=ct\cosh\phi - x\sinh\phict′=ctcoshϕ−xsinhϕ, x′=xcosh⁡ϕ−ctsinh⁡ϕx'=x\cosh\phi-ct\sinh\phix′=xcoshϕ−ctsinhϕ.

6.2 · Rapidities add

Multiply two of them:

(cosh⁡ϕ2−sinh⁡ϕ2−sinh⁡ϕ2cosh⁡ϕ2)(cosh⁡ϕ1−sinh⁡ϕ1−sinh⁡ϕ1cosh⁡ϕ1)=  (c1c2+s1s2−(s1c2+c1s2)−(c1s2+s1c2)s1s2+c1c2), \begin{aligned} &\begin{pmatrix} \cosh\phi_{2} & -\sinh\phi_{2}\\ -\sinh\phi_{2} & \cosh\phi_{2}\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \cosh\phi_{1} & -\sinh\phi_{1}\\ -\sinh\phi_{1} & \cosh\phi_{1}\end{pmatrix}\\[6pt] &\qquad=\; \begin{pmatrix} c_{1}c_{2}+s_{1}s_{2} & -(s_{1}c_{2}+c_{1}s_{2})\\ -(c_{1}s_{2}+s_{1}c_{2}) & s_{1}s_{2}+c_{1}c_{2}\end{pmatrix}, \end{aligned} ​(coshϕ2​−sinhϕ2​​−sinhϕ2​coshϕ2​​)(coshϕ1​−sinhϕ1​​−sinhϕ1​coshϕ1​​)=(c1​c2​+s1​s2​−(c1​s2​+s1​c2​)​−(s1​c2​+c1​s2​)s1​s2​+c1​c2​​),​ (2.2.49)

writing ci=cosh⁡ϕic_{i}=\cosh\phi_{i}ci​=coshϕi​, si=sinh⁡ϕis_{i}=\sinh\phi_{i}si​=sinhϕi​. The hyperbolic addition formulas — cosh⁡(a+b)=cosh⁡acosh⁡b+sinh⁡asinh⁡b\cosh(a+b)=\cosh a\cosh b+\sinh a\sinh bcosh(a+b)=coshacoshb+sinhasinhb and sinh⁡(a+b)=sinh⁡acosh⁡b+cosh⁡asinh⁡b\sinh(a+b)=\sinh a\cosh b+\cosh a\sinh bsinh(a+b)=sinhacoshb+coshasinhb — turn that into

  Λ(ϕ2) Λ(ϕ1)  =  Λ(ϕ1+ϕ2).   \boxed{\;\Lambda(\phi_{2})\,\Lambda(\phi_{1}) \;=\; \Lambda(\phi_{1}+\phi_{2}).\;} Λ(ϕ2​)Λ(ϕ1​)=Λ(ϕ1​+ϕ2​).​ (2.2.50)

Rapidities add. Plainly, exactly, with no correction term. And taking tanh⁡\tanhtanh of both sides recovers (2.2.26), since tanh⁡(ϕ1+ϕ2)=(tanh⁡ϕ1+tanh⁡ϕ2)/(1+tanh⁡ϕ1tanh⁡ϕ2)\tanh(\phi_{1}+\phi_{2})=(\tanh\phi_{1}+\tanh\phi_{2})/(1+\tanh\phi_{1}\tanh\phi_{2})tanh(ϕ1​+ϕ2​)=(tanhϕ1​+tanhϕ2​)/(1+tanhϕ1​tanhϕ2​) — so §5 and §6 are the same statement written in two variables.

Check the arithmetic of (2.2.28) in the new currency: artanh⁡(0.5)=0.549306\operatorname{artanh}(0.5)=0.549306artanh(0.5)=0.549306, twice that is 1.098612=ln⁡31.098612=\ln31.098612=ln3, and tanh⁡(ln⁡3)=(3−13)/(3+13)=0.8\tanh(\ln3)= (3-\tfrac13)/(3+\tfrac13)=0.8tanh(ln3)=(3−31​)/(3+31​)=0.8 ✓. Two boosts of 0.5c0.5c0.5c do not give ccc; they give rapidity 2×0.54932\times0.54932×0.5493, which is velocity 0.8c0.8c0.8c.

The moral

Velocities "fail to add" for the same reason angles-as-slopes fail to add. Compose two rotations and their angles add; their slopes combine by (m1+m2)/(1−m1m2)(m_{1}+m_{2})/(1-m_{1}m_{2})(m1​+m2​)/(1−m1​m2​), which nobody finds shocking because nobody expected slopes to be the natural parameter. Velocity is the slope of a worldline. Rapidity is its angle. We spent three hundred years adding the slopes.

And the change of variable makes the light barrier trivial rather than mysterious. Rapidity runs over the whole of R\RR and adds without limit; you can boost forever. But β=tanh⁡ϕ\beta=\tanh\phiβ=tanhϕ saturates: ϕ=1\phi=1ϕ=1 gives β=0.762\beta=0.762β=0.762, ϕ=3\phi=3ϕ=3 gives 0.9950.9950.995, ϕ=10\phi=10ϕ=10 gives 0.99999999590.99999999590.9999999959. The barrier is not a barrier at all — it is the horizontal asymptote of tanh⁡\tanhtanh, seen from inside a badly chosen coordinate.

Two forward pointers, flagged ⚑

(a) This is a Lie group in embryo. The boosts along one axis are a family Λ(ϕ)\Lambda(\phi)Λ(ϕ) with Λ(0)=I\Lambda(0)=IΛ(0)=I, Λ(ϕ2)Λ(ϕ1)=Λ(ϕ1+ϕ2)\Lambda(\phi_{2})\Lambda(\phi_{1})=\Lambda(\phi_{1}+\phi_{2})Λ(ϕ2​)Λ(ϕ1​)=Λ(ϕ1​+ϕ2​) and Λ\LambdaΛ smooth in ϕ\phiϕ — a smooth one-parameter group. ⚑ Chapter 6.1 shows that any such family is Λ(ϕ)=exp⁡(ϕK)\Lambda(\phi)=\exp(\phi K)Λ(ϕ)=exp(ϕK) for a fixed matrix KKK, its generator, obtained by differentiating at the identity. Here K=dΛdϕ∣0=(0−1−10)K = \dv{\Lambda}{\phi}\big|_{0} = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}0 & -1\\ -1 & 0\end{smallmatrix}\right)K=dϕdΛ​​0​=(0−1​−10​), and indeed K2=IK^{2}=IK2=I, so exp⁡(ϕK)=Icosh⁡ϕ+Ksinh⁡ϕ\exp(\phi K)=I\cosh\phi + K\sinh\phiexp(ϕK)=Icoshϕ+Ksinhϕ, which is (2.2.48) exactly. The full Lorentz group has six such parameters — three boosts, three rotations — and is called SO(1,3)\mathrm{SO}(1,3)SO(1,3).

(b) The hyperbolic functions are the metric's minus sign, surfacing. A rotation in the xyxyxy plane is (cos⁡θ−sin⁡θsin⁡θcos⁡θ)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\cos\theta & -\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta\end{smallmatrix}\right)(cosθsinθ​−sinθcosθ​) and preserves x2+y2x^{2}+y^{2}x2+y2. A boost in the (ct,x)(ct,x)(ct,x) plane is (2.2.48) and preserves c2t2−x2c^{2}t^{2}-x^{2}c2t2−x2, per (2.2.20). Circular functions preserve a sum of squares; hyperbolic functions preserve a difference. The two matrices differ in exactly one respect: the rotation's off-diagonal entries carry opposite signs, the boost's carry the same sign — the boost matrix is symmetric, the rotation's off-diagonal part is not. That single sign is the −-− in ημν=diag(1,−1,−1,−1)\eta_{\mu\nu}=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)ημν​=diag(1,−1,−1,−1). Chapter 2.3 makes this geometric: a boost is a rotation through an imaginary angle, or better, an honest rotation in a geometry whose circles are hyperbolas.

Grind box — hyperbolic functions from scratch, in case they are rusty

Definitions, and everything else follows:

cosh⁡ϕ=eϕ+e−ϕ2,sinh⁡ϕ=eϕ−e−ϕ2,tanh⁡ϕ=sinh⁡ϕcosh⁡ϕ. \cosh\phi = \frac{\ee^{\phi}+\ee^{-\phi}}{2}, \qquad \sinh\phi = \frac{\ee^{\phi}-\ee^{-\phi}}{2}, \qquad \tanh\phi=\frac{\sinh\phi}{\cosh\phi}. coshϕ=2eϕ+e−ϕ​,sinhϕ=2eϕ−e−ϕ​,tanhϕ=coshϕsinhϕ​.

The Pythagorean identity. Multiply out:

cosh⁡2ϕ−sinh⁡2ϕ=(eϕ+e−ϕ)2−(eϕ−e−ϕ)24=4 eϕe−ϕ4=1. \cosh^{2}\phi-\sinh^{2}\phi = \frac{\big(\ee^{\phi}+\ee^{-\phi}\big)^{2}-\big(\ee^{\phi}-\ee^{-\phi}\big)^{2}}{4} = \frac{4\,\ee^{\phi}\ee^{-\phi}}{4} = 1. cosh2ϕ−sinh2ϕ=4(eϕ+e−ϕ)2−(eϕ−e−ϕ)2​=44eϕe−ϕ​=1.

Compare cos⁡2+sin⁡2=1\cos^{2}+\sin^{2}=1cos2+sin2=1: the point (cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)(cosθ,sinθ) traces a circle, the point (cosh⁡ϕ,sinh⁡ϕ)(\cosh\phi,\sinh\phi)(coshϕ,sinhϕ) traces a hyperbola. That hyperbola is Chapter 2.3's central object.

Addition. Multiply exponentials:

cosh⁡acosh⁡b+sinh⁡asinh⁡b=14[(ea+e−a)(eb+e−b)+(ea−e−a)(eb−e−b)]=14[2ea+b+2e−a−b]  =  cosh⁡(a+b). \begin{aligned} \cosh a\cosh b + \sinh a \sinh b &= \tfrac14\Big[\big(\ee^{a}+\ee^{-a}\big)\big(\ee^{b}+\ee^{-b}\big) + \big(\ee^{a}-\ee^{-a}\big)\big(\ee^{b}-\ee^{-b}\big)\Big]\\[3pt] &= \tfrac14\Big[2\ee^{a+b}+2\ee^{-a-b}\Big] \;=\; \cosh(a+b). \end{aligned} coshacoshb+sinhasinhb​=41​[(ea+e−a)(eb+e−b)+(ea−e−a)(eb−e−b)]=41​[2ea+b+2e−a−b]=cosh(a+b).​

The sinh⁡\sinhsinh formula goes the same way. Dividing them gives the tanh⁡\tanhtanh addition theorem, which is (2.2.45).

The inverse. Solve β=tanh⁡ϕ\beta=\tanh\phiβ=tanhϕ for ϕ\phiϕ. Writing w=e2ϕw=\ee^{2\phi}w=e2ϕ,

β=eϕ−e−ϕeϕ+e−ϕ=w−1w+1  ⟹  w=1+β1−β  ⟹  ϕ=12ln⁡1+β1−β. \beta = \frac{\ee^{\phi}-\ee^{-\phi}}{\ee^{\phi}+\ee^{-\phi}} = \frac{w-1}{w+1} \;\Longrightarrow\; w = \frac{1+\beta}{1-\beta} \;\Longrightarrow\; \phi = \tfrac12\ln\frac{1+\beta}{1-\beta}. β=eϕ+e−ϕeϕ−e−ϕ​=w+1w−1​⟹w=1−β1+β​⟹ϕ=21​ln1−β1+β​.

Useful values: artanh⁡(0.5)=0.5493\operatorname{artanh}(0.5)=0.5493artanh(0.5)=0.5493, artanh⁡(0.8)=1.0986=ln⁡3\operatorname{artanh}(0.8)=1.0986=\ln3artanh(0.8)=1.0986=ln3, artanh⁡(0.9)=1.4722\operatorname{artanh}(0.9)=1.4722artanh(0.9)=1.4722, artanh⁡(0.99)=2.6467\operatorname{artanh}(0.99)=2.6467artanh(0.99)=2.6467. Note how slowly rapidity grows once β\betaβ is close to 111 — going from 0.9c0.9c0.9c to 0.99c0.99c0.99c costs about 1.171.171.17 of rapidity, roughly the same as going from rest to 0.8c0.8c0.8c. In Chapter 2.5 that observation acquires teeth: the energy needed is what grows without bound.

Derivatives. cosh⁡′=sinh⁡\cosh'=\sinhcosh′=sinh, sinh⁡′=cosh⁡\sinh'=\coshsinh′=cosh, tanh⁡′=1/cosh⁡2=1−tanh⁡2\tanh'=1/\cosh^{2}=1-\tanh^{2}tanh′=1/cosh2=1−tanh2, all immediate from the exponential definitions. Problem 4 uses the last one.

In plain terms 2.2.6

Compose two rotations of a plane and their angles add, as anybody expects of a family labelled by one number. Boosts along an axis are such a family, so something of theirs adds, and it is not velocity. Take the composition rule seriously and it is a formula everybody has seen, the addition theorem for the hyperbolic tangent, so what adds is the angle whose hyperbolic tangent the velocity is.

Call that angle the rapidity. Rapidities add exactly, with no correction term, and their matrices multiply the way two turns of a plane do. This collects the pairing between a generator and the family it builds, promised when a self-partnered map was first exponentiated and again when conserved quantities were made to push things around: one fixed matrix, exponentiated by the parameter, generates the family.

Why velocities looked defective is now visible, and it is not a fact about nature. Velocity is the slope of a worldline and rapidity is its angle, and slopes have never added: two turns of a plane combine their angles cleanly while their slopes combine by an ugly quotient that shocks nobody, since nobody expected slopes to be the natural label. Three centuries were spent adding the slopes. The barrier stops being mysterious in the same stroke, since the angle runs over every real number and adds without limit while its hyperbolic tangent creeps towards one and never arrives.

7 · The paradoxes, dismantled

There are perhaps a dozen famous special-relativity paradoxes and they are all the same paradox. Here are the two that matter, worked to the bottom, and then the general statement.

7.1 · The twin paradox

The setup. Two twins, both aged 202020. One stays on Earth. The other flies to a star 444 light-years away at β=0.8\beta=0.8β=0.8 (γ=5/3\gamma=5/3γ=5/3), turns round, and comes back. Earth-frame arithmetic: the outbound leg takes 4/0.8=54/0.8=54/0.8=5 years, the trip takes 101010 years, and by (2.2.31) the traveller's clock — moving — records 10/γ=10×0.6=610/\gamma = 10\times0.6 = 610/γ=10×0.6=6 years. The traveller returns aged 262626, the stay-at-home is 303030.

The apparent paradox, stated as sharply as it deserves. Motion is relative. From the traveller's point of view, Earth receded at 0.8c0.8c0.8c and came back. By §4.2, each observer finds the other's clock slow — symmetrically, by the same γ\gammaγ. So the traveller should equally conclude that Earth's clock ran slow throughout: his own 666 years, divided by γ=5/3\gamma=5/3γ=5/3, gives 3.63.63.6 years for the Earth twin, who should therefore be the younger one on his return. Both cannot be true: when the two stand next to each other at the end, comparing wrinkles is a local coincidence, and there is one fact of the matter.

Where the symmetry fails. It fails at the turnaround, and it fails physically, not verbally. The stay-at-home twin occupies a single inertial frame for the whole story. The traveller does not: he is at rest in one inertial frame going out and a different one coming back. The switch is detectable from inside the ship without looking out of the window — an accelerometer registers it, coffee spills, the traveller is pressed into his seat. There is no symmetry to appeal to, because the two histories are physically different, and no amount of "motion is relative" makes them the same. One worldline is straight; the other has a kink.

That is the resolution in one sentence, and people rightly find it unsatisfying, because it explains why the twins may differ without showing where the missing 6.46.46.4 years went — the gap between the traveller's naive 3.63.63.6 and the actual 101010. So track them.

Following the traveller's own accounting, year by year

Work in Earth-frame coordinates (ct,x)(ct,x)(ct,x) measured in light-years and years, with the departure at the origin. The turnaround is the event T=(ct,x)=(5,4)T=(ct,x)=(5,4)T=(ct,x)=(5,4).

Outbound leg. The traveller is at rest in the frame S′S'S′ moving at β=+0.8\beta=+0.8β=+0.8. His own elapsed time is, from (2.2.19) applied to the event TTT,

ctT′=γ(ctT−βxT)=53(5−0.8×4)=53×1.8=3 years. ct'_{T} = \gamma\big(ct_{T}-\beta x_{T}\big) = \tfrac53\big(5-0.8\times4\big) = \tfrac53\times1.8 = 3\ \text{years}. ctT′​=γ(ctT​−βxT​)=35​(5−0.8×4)=35​×1.8=3 years. (2.2.51)

Which of Earth's events does he call simultaneous with his turnaround? Those with the same t′t't′, i.e. ct−βx=1.8ct-\beta x = 1.8ct−βx=1.8. On Earth x=0x=0x=0, so

ctEarth=1.8 years. ct_{\text{Earth}} = 1.8\ \text{years}. ctEarth​=1.8 years. (2.2.52)

Consistent with time dilation as the traveller sees it: his 333 years, divided by γ=5/3\gamma=5/3γ=5/3, gives 1.81.81.8 years on the Earth clock. From out there, Earth is the moving one and Earth is running slow. ✓

Inbound leg. After the turn he is at rest in S′′S''S′′ moving at β=−0.8\beta=-0.8β=−0.8. Its simultaneity slices are ct+βx=constct+\beta x = \text{const}ct+βx=const, and through the same turnaround event T=(5,4)T=(5,4)T=(5,4),

ct+0.8x=5+3.2=8.2⟹ctEarth=8.2 years. ct + 0.8x = 5 + 3.2 = 8.2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad ct_{\text{Earth}} = 8.2\ \text{years}. ct+0.8x=5+3.2=8.2⟹ctEarth​=8.2 years. (2.2.53)

The jump. An instant before the turn, the traveller's "now on Earth" is year 1.81.81.8. An instant after, it is year 8.28.28.2. Nothing happened to Earth; the traveller changed which slice of spacetime he calls "now", and the slice swung through Earth's worldline:

Δtjump=8.2−1.8=6.4 years  =  2βLc  =  2×0.8×4. \Delta t_{\text{jump}} = 8.2 - 1.8 = 6.4\ \text{years} \;=\; \frac{2\beta L}{c} \;=\; 2\times0.8\times4. Δtjump​=8.2−1.8=6.4 years=c2βL​=2×0.8×4. (2.2.54)

Now the books balance exactly:

1.8⏟outbound  +  6.4⏟turnaround jump  +  1.8⏟inbound  =  10.0 years✓ \underbrace{1.8}_{\text{outbound}} \;+\; \underbrace{6.4}_{\text{turnaround jump}} \;+\; \underbrace{1.8}_{\text{inbound}} \;=\; 10.0\ \text{years} \quad\checkmark outbound1.8​​+turnaround jump6.4​​+inbound1.8​​=10.0 years✓ (2.2.55)

while the traveller's own clock reads 3+3=63+3=63+3=6 years. Every year is accounted for. The traveller's claim "Earth's clock ran slow" was correct on each leg; what he cannot do is stitch the two legs' notions of "now" together and pretend they were one. The naive symmetric argument gave Earth 1.8+1.8=3.61.8+1.8=3.61.8+1.8=3.6 years, and the 6.46.46.4 it was missing is exactly the span his simultaneity slice swept across Earth's worldline during the turn — the one moment at which he was not an inertial observer, and therefore the one moment at which his slices were not entitled to line up.

The version to actually remember

Forget clocks for a moment. Proper time is the length of a worldline: between two events, Δτ=Δt2−Δx2/c2\Delta\tau=\sqrt{\Delta t^{2}-\Delta x^{2}/c^{2}}Δτ=Δt2−Δx2/c2​ along each straight piece, and you add the pieces. Two different paths between the same two endpoints have different lengths. Nobody is scandalised that a detour through the next town adds mileage.

Check the twin numbers this way. Straight path: Δτ=102−0=10\Delta\tau=\sqrt{10^{2}-0}=10Δτ=102−0​=10 years. Bent path, two legs: 52−42=3\sqrt{5^{2}-4^{2}}=352−42​=3 each, total 666. Same endpoints, different lengths, no paradox — and no need to mention acceleration at all, except to say that a kink is what makes a path longer or shorter than a straight one.

The one genuinely strange thing is the sign. Because of the minus in Δt2−Δx2/c2\Delta t^{2}-\Delta x^{2}/c^{2}Δt2−Δx2/c2, the straight path is the one with the most proper time, not the least. Detours in spacetime save you time rather than costing it. That inverted extremum is not a curiosity; it is the principle from which Chapter 3.1 derives the motion of freely falling bodies, and it is why a satellite's orbit is the path that maximises the proper time of the clock aboard it.

Turn on the twin toggle in the figure above and watch this happen. The traveller's two simultaneity slices are the green dashed lines through the turnaround; where they cross x=0x=0x=0 they bracket exactly the jump. Drag β\betaβ and the numbers move, but the three pieces always sum to the stay-at-home twin's total.

7.2 · The pole and the barn

The setup. A runner carries a pole of proper length 15 m15\ \mathrm{m}15 m through a barn of proper length 10 m10\ \mathrm{m}10 m with a door at each end, at β=0.8\beta=0.8β=0.8 so γ=5/3\gamma=5/3γ=5/3. In the barn's frame the pole is contracted to 15×0.6=9 m15\times0.6=9\ \mathrm{m}15×0.6=9 m: it fits, with a metre to spare. The farmer shuts both doors simultaneously at the moment it is inside, and — this is the claim to be tested — the pole is briefly wholly enclosed.

The apparent paradox. In the runner's frame the pole is 15 m15\ \mathrm{m}15 m and the barn is contracted to 10×0.6=6 m10\times0.6=6\ \mathrm{m}10×0.6=6 m. The pole is two and a half times the barn's length. It cannot possibly be enclosed. But "the pole was inside the barn with both doors shut" ought to be a fact, not an opinion.

The resolution. It is not a fact, because it is not a local coincidence. It is a statement about two events at different places — front door shuts and back door shuts — being simultaneous. By §4.1 that is frame-dependent, and here the disagreement is enormous: with Δx=10 m\Delta x = 10\ \mathrm{m}Δx=10 m,

c Δt′=−γβ Δx=−53×0.8×10=−403=−13.33 m, c\,\Delta t' = -\gamma\beta\,\Delta x = -\tfrac53\times0.8\times10 = -\tfrac{40}{3} = -13.33\ \mathrm{m}, cΔt′=−γβΔx=−35​×0.8×10=−340​=−13.33 m, (2.2.56)

The two door-closings are 13.33 m13.33\ \mathrm{m}13.33 m of light travel — that is, 44.5 ns44.5\ \mathrm{ns}44.5 ns — apart in the runner's frame, with the far door going first. They do not shut together at all. The far door shuts and reopens long before the pole's nose gets there; much later, the near door shuts behind the pole's tail. The pole passes through a barn that is opening and closing around it like a slow shutter, and it is never enclosed for an instant.

Both frames are right, and — the decisive point — they agree on everything that is not a convention. Was the pole ever hit by a door? No, in both frames. Did the nose emerge from the far door before the far door shut? Problem 2 tabulates every event in both frames and the answer is the same in both. What they disagree on is only "did the two doors shut at the same time", which is not an observable but a labelling.

7.3 · The general lesson

Every special-relativity paradox is the same paradox

Somewhere in the statement, someone has assumed simultaneity is absolute. Find that assumption and the paradox dissolves. There is no second mechanism.

The reliable procedure, which will get you through any of them:

  1. List the events. Not objects, not "the rod" or "the ship" — events, each with a definite (t,x)(t,x)(t,x) in one frame. Anything that is not an event is not yet a physics question.
  2. Ask which claims are local coincidences. Two things at the same place at the same time: a door hitting a pole, two clocks side by side, a twin shaking a hand. These are frame-independent and every frame must agree on them, full stop.
  3. Transform. Apply (2.2.19) to each event and tabulate.
  4. Locate the smuggled assumption. It will be a claim of the form "and at that moment, over there, ..." — a statement about distant simultaneity dressed as a fact.

Apply that to the twins (the smuggled claim: "while the traveller aged 3 years, Earth aged 1.8, and that was still true after the turn"), to the pole (the smuggled claim: "both doors shut at the same time" as an absolute), or to any of the others — the ladder and the trapdoor, the rigid rod pushed at one end, the submarine that both sinks and floats. Same disease, same cure, every time.

In plain terms 2.2.7

One twin comes back younger than the other, and the asymmetry permitting it is physical rather than verbal. The one who stayed occupied a single inertial frame throughout; the one who travelled was at rest in one frame going out and in a different one coming back, and the switch is detectable from inside the ship, with no window needed. One history is bent and the other is not.

Saying so explains why the two may differ without showing where the missing years went, and they can be tracked. The traveller's claim that the other clock was running slow is correct on each leg taken separately. What he may not do is stitch the two legs' notions of the present together, because at the turn his family of nows swings through an enormous span of the other worldline, and that span is precisely the amount the naive accounting was missing.

Every paradox in the subject is this one in different clothes. Somewhere in the statement, someone has treated the simultaneity of two distant events as a fact rather than a labelling, and the cure never varies. List the events; ask which claims are local coincidences of one thing with another at one place, since everybody agrees on those; transform the rest; and the smuggled assumption will be standing in plain view. What this pile of results is waiting for is the idea that organises it.

8 · Worked examples

Worked example 1 — cosmic-ray muons, done in both frames

Muons are produced by cosmic-ray collisions about 15 km15\ \mathrm{km}15 km up in the atmosphere. ⚑ Their mean lifetime at rest is τ0=2.2 μs\tau_{0}=2.2\ \mathrm{\mu s}τ0​=2.2 μs, measured in the laboratory, and they decay exponentially: the fraction surviving after a proper time τ\tauτ is e−τ/τ0\ee^{-\tau/\tau_{0}}e−τ/τ0​ (Chapter 0.1 §5 — same first-order kinetics as drug clearance). Take β=0.998\beta=0.998β=0.998. What fraction reaches sea level, according to (a) Newtonian expectations and (b) relativity? Then redo (b) entirely in the muon's frame, where the atmosphere is contracted rather than the clock dilated, and check the two accounts agree.

Step 0 — the Lorentz factor.

γ=11−0.9982=13.996×10−3=15.82. \gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-0.998^{2}}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3.996\times10^{-3}}} = 15.82. γ=1−0.9982​1​=3.996×10−3​1​=15.82.

Step 1 — Newtonian. No dilation, no contraction: the muon crosses 15 km15\ \mathrm{km}15 km at 0.998c0.998c0.998c, and its internal clock is the same as ours.

t=15 0000.998×2.998×108=5.013×10−5 s=50.13 μs, t = \frac{15\,000}{0.998\times2.998\times10^{8}} = 5.013\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{s} = 50.13\ \mathrm{\mu s}, t=0.998×2.998×10815000​=5.013×10−5 s=50.13 μs,

which is 50.13/2.2=22.7950.13/2.2 = 22.7950.13/2.2=22.79 lifetimes. Surviving fraction:

e−22.79=1.27×10−10. \ee^{-22.79} = 1.27\times10^{-10}. e−22.79=1.27×10−10.

About one muon in eight billion. The predicted flux at sea level is, to any instrument ever built, zero. ⚑ What is actually observed is a copious flux — of order one muon per square centimetre per minute at sea level. The Newtonian prediction is not slightly wrong.

Step 2 — relativity, told from the ground. The muon's internal clock is the moving one, so by (2.2.31) the proper time it experiences during our 50.13 μs50.13\ \mathrm{\mu s}50.13 μs is

Δτ=Δtγ=50.1315.82=3.169 μs=1.441 lifetimes, \Delta\tau = \frac{\Delta t}{\gamma} = \frac{50.13}{15.82} = 3.169\ \mathrm{\mu s} = 1.441\ \text{lifetimes}, Δτ=γΔt​=15.8250.13​=3.169 μs=1.441 lifetimes, e−1.441=0.2368. \ee^{-1.441} = 0.2368. e−1.441=0.2368.

Nearly a quarter of them make it. The two predictions differ by a factor of 1.9×1091.9\times10^{9}1.9×109 — which is why this is not a subtle test but a demonstration you can do with a scintillator on a bench, and why ⚑ Rossi and Hall's 1941 mountain-versus-sea-level muon counts were decisive.

Step 3 — the same physics, told from the muon. This is the half that gets skipped, and it is the half that matters, because in the muon's own frame nothing dilates its clock. Its clock is at rest. It lives 2.2 μs2.2\ \mathrm{\mu s}2.2 μs on average, exactly as advertised — and it had better still reach the ground, because whether a given muon arrives is a local coincidence and frames are not allowed to disagree about it.

What is different in the muon's frame is the atmosphere, which is now the moving object. By (2.2.35), the 15 km15\ \mathrm{km}15 km column of air — proper length, since it is at rest relative to the ground — is contracted to

L=L0γ=15 00015.82=948.2 m. L = \frac{L_{0}}{\gamma} = \frac{15\,000}{15.82} = 948.2\ \mathrm{m}. L=γL0​​=15.8215000​=948.2 m.

That column rushes past the muon at 0.998c0.998c0.998c, taking

Δtmuon=948.20.998×2.998×108=3.169 μs, \Delta t_{\text{muon}} = \frac{948.2}{0.998\times2.998\times10^{8}} = 3.169\ \mathrm{\mu s}, Δtmuon​=0.998×2.998×108948.2​=3.169 μs,

and the surviving fraction is e−3.169/2.2=e−1.441=0.2368\ee^{-3.169/2.2}=\ee^{-1.441}=0.2368e−3.169/2.2=e−1.441=0.2368. Identical. ✓

What this teaches. The two frames disagree about why the muon survives — one says the clock ran slow, the other says the trip was short — and agree exactly on the observable, which is the number of muons per second landing on the detector. That is the correct relationship between frames in every problem in this chapter: mechanisms are frame-dependent, observables are not. Note also that neither account works without the other's ingredient: use dilation and contraction together and you would double-count by a factor of γ\gammaγ; use neither and you get 10−1010^{-10}10−10. There is exactly one factor of γ\gammaγ in the problem, and each frame places it somewhere different.

Worked example 2 — closing speed versus relative speed

In a laboratory, two particles fly directly toward each other, each at 0.9c0.9c0.9c as measured in the lab. (a) At what rate does the gap between them close, in lab coordinates? (b) What is the speed of one as measured in the rest frame of the other? (c) Reconcile.

(a) The closing rate. In lab coordinates, particle 1 is at x1=−d/2+0.9ctx_{1}=-d/2+0.9ctx1​=−d/2+0.9ct and particle 2 at x2=d/2−0.9ctx_{2}=d/2-0.9ctx2​=d/2−0.9ct. The gap is x2−x1=d−1.8ctx_{2}-x_{1}=d-1.8ctx2​−x1​=d−1.8ct, so

−ddt(x2−x1)=1.8 c. -\dv{}{t}\big(x_{2}-x_{1}\big) = 1.8\,c. −dtd​(x2​−x1​)=1.8c.

The gap shrinks at 1.8c1.8c1.8c. This is correct and no rule is violated. It is not the speed of anything; it is the rate of change of a difference of two coordinates, both measured in one frame. Nothing is transported at 1.8c1.8c1.8c — as in §5's spotlight, ask what is being carried, and the answer is nothing.

(b) The relative speed. This is a different question: what does particle 2's own frame measure for particle 1? Take S′S'S′ to be particle 2's rest frame, so βv=−0.9\beta_{v}=-0.9βv​=−0.9 (it moves in the −x-x−x direction in the lab), and the object of interest has βu=+0.9\beta_{u}=+0.9βu​=+0.9. Then by (2.2.40),

βu′=βu−βv1−βuβv=0.9−(−0.9)1−(0.9)(−0.9)=1.81.81=0.994475. \beta_{u'} = \frac{\beta_{u}-\beta_{v}}{1-\beta_{u}\beta_{v}} = \frac{0.9-(-0.9)}{1-(0.9)(-0.9)} = \frac{1.8}{1.81} = 0.994475. βu′​=1−βu​βv​βu​−βv​​=1−(0.9)(−0.9)0.9−(−0.9)​=1.811.8​=0.994475.

So u′=0.9945 cu' = 0.9945\,cu′=0.9945c. Not 1.8c1.8c1.8c; not even ccc. Each particle sees the other approaching at 99.45%99.45\%99.45% of light speed.

Cross-check with rapidity. artanh⁡(0.9)=1.472219\operatorname{artanh}(0.9)=1.472219artanh(0.9)=1.472219, and the relative rapidity is the sum, 2×1.472219=2.9444392\times1.472219=2.9444392×1.472219=2.944439. Then tanh⁡(2.944439)=0.994475\tanh(2.944439)=0.994475tanh(2.944439)=0.994475 ✓ — the same number, obtained by addition rather than by a formula with a denominator in it. This is §6 earning its keep.

(c) Reconciling. The two answers are answers to two different questions, and the language of everyday physics does not distinguish them because at low speed they coincide: for β≪1\beta\ll1β≪1, βu′≈βu−βv\beta_{u'}\approx\beta_{u}-\beta_{v}βu′​≈βu​−βv​, which is the closing rate. At high speed they separate dramatically. The rule: a closing rate is a statement about one frame's coordinates and can be up to 2c2c2c; a relative velocity is a statement about one object's rest frame and is always less than ccc. Only the second one is a velocity in the sense that (2.2.40) and Chapter 2.5's dynamics care about.

Why the difference has teeth. In a collider the quantity that determines what you can produce is the energy in the centre-of-mass frame, which depends on the relative velocity, not the closing rate. Two beams at 0.9c0.9c0.9c head-on do not collide at 1.8c1.8c1.8c in any useful sense; they collide at a relative γ\gammaγ of cosh⁡(2.944)=9.53\cosh(2.944)=9.53cosh(2.944)=9.53, which is γrel=γ1γ2(1+β1β2)=2.2942×1.81=9.53\gamma_{\text{rel}} = \gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}(1+\beta_{1}\beta_{2}) = 2.294^{2}\times1.81 = 9.53γrel​=γ1​γ2​(1+β1​β2​)=2.2942×1.81=9.53 ✓ — the composition law of §3, doing an accelerator physicist's arithmetic.

Problem 1 — the transverse velocity, which changes even though y′=yy'=yy′=y

An object has velocity components (ux,uy)(u_{x},u_{y})(ux​,uy​) in SSS. Derive ux′u'_{x}ux′​ and uy′u'_{y}uy′​ in S′S'S′. Explain why uy′≠uyu'_{y}\neq u_{y}uy′​=uy​ even though the yyy coordinate itself is untouched. Then check the formula on light: a pulse moving in the +y+y+y direction at speed ccc in SSS — verify that S′S'S′ also measures speed ccc, and find the angle by which the pulse's direction is tilted.

Solution

Derivation. Take differentials of (2.2.19) including the transverse equation dy′=dy\dd y'=\dd ydy′=dy:

dx′=γ(dx−vdt),dy′=dy,dt′=γ(dt−v dxc2). \dd x' = \gamma\big(\dd x - v\dd t\big), \qquad \dd y' = \dd y, \qquad \dd t' = \gamma\left(\dd t - \frac{v\,\dd x}{c^{2}}\right). dx′=γ(dx−vdt),dy′=dy,dt′=γ(dt−c2vdx​).

Divide dy′\dd y'dy′ by dt′\dd t'dt′ and then divide numerator and denominator by dt\dd tdt:

uy′=dyγ(dt−vdx/c2)=uyγ(1−uxvc2),ux′=ux−v1−uxvc2. u'_{y} = \frac{\dd y}{\gamma\big(\dd t - v\dd x/c^{2}\big)} = \frac{u_{y}}{\gamma\left(1-\dfrac{u_{x}v}{c^{2}}\right)}, \qquad u'_{x} = \frac{u_{x}-v}{1-\dfrac{u_{x}v}{c^{2}}}. uy′​=γ(dt−vdx/c2)dy​=γ(1−c2ux​v​)uy​​,ux′​=1−c2ux​v​ux​−v​.

Why it changes. A velocity is a ratio, Δy/Δt\Delta y/\Delta tΔy/Δt. The numerator is indeed untouched — but the denominator is not. Time intervals transform, so a displacement that is unchanged, divided by a duration that is not, gives a changed rate. The lesson generalises far beyond this problem: an invariant numerator does not make an invariant quotient, which is exactly why Chapter 2.5 will insist on differentiating with respect to proper time rather than coordinate time when it builds the four-velocity.

The special case ux=0u_{x}=0ux​=0. Then ux′=−vu'_{x}=-vux′​=−v and uy′=uy/γu'_{y}=u_{y}/\gammauy′​=uy​/γ: the transverse velocity is reduced by exactly γ\gammaγ, since the transverse displacement is unchanged while the time to make it is dilated.

Check on light. Put ux=0u_{x}=0ux​=0, uy=cu_{y}=cuy​=c. Then ux′=−vu'_{x}=-vux′​=−v and uy′=c/γu'_{y}=c/\gammauy′​=c/γ, so

∣u′∣2=v2+c2γ2=v2+c2(1−β2)=v2+c2−v2=c2. \abs{u'}^{2} = v^{2} + \frac{c^{2}}{\gamma^{2}} = v^{2} + c^{2}\big(1-\beta^{2}\big) = v^{2}+c^{2}-v^{2} = c^{2}. ∣u′∣2=v2+γ2c2​=v2+c2(1−β2)=v2+c2−v2=c2.

Speed ccc ✓ — and note how the two pieces conspire: the v2v^{2}v2 gained along xxx is precisely the c2β2c^{2}\beta^{2}c2β2 lost along yyy. Postulate 2 again, checking itself in a direction we never imposed it.

The tilt. The direction makes an angle θ′\theta'θ′ with the y′y'y′-axis given by

tan⁡θ′=∣ux′∣uy′=vc/γ=γβ,equivalentlysin⁡θ′=β. \tan\theta' = \frac{\abs{u'_{x}}}{u'_{y}} = \frac{v}{c/\gamma} = \gamma\beta, \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \sin\theta' = \beta. tanθ′=uy′​∣ux′​∣​=c/γv​=γβ,equivalentlysinθ′=β.

This is stellar aberration: the apparent position of a star shifts by θ′≈β\theta'\approx\betaθ′≈β as the Earth's velocity changes around its orbit, giving an annual ellipse of angular radius β=9.94×10−5 rad\beta = 9.94\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{rad}β=9.94×10−5 rad, which in arcseconds (× 206265\times\,206265×206265) is 20.5′′20.5''20.5′′. Bradley measured it in 1727, and it was one of the constraints Chapter 2.1 §6.1 used to kill the fully dragged ether. Chapter 2.1's Problem 3 obtained θ≈v/c\theta\approx v/cθ≈v/c from a first-order argument; sin⁡θ′=β\sin\theta'=\betasinθ′=β is the exact statement, and the two agree to one part in 10810^{8}108 at the Earth's orbital speed. Note also that sin⁡θ′=β\sin\theta'=\betasinθ′=β is the same relation as the Terrell–Penrose rotation angle in §4.3 — not a coincidence, since both are the statement that a boost tilts light rays.

Problem 2 — the pole and the barn, with every event tabulated

Pole of proper length 15 m15\ \mathrm{m}15 m, barn of proper length 10 m10\ \mathrm{m}10 m with doors at x=0x=0x=0 (entrance) and x=10 mx=10\ \mathrm{m}x=10 m (exit), runner at β=0.8\beta=0.8β=0.8 in the +x+x+x direction. Use coordinates (ct,x)(ct,x)(ct,x) with both in metres. Let event AAA — the pole's tail reaching the entrance — be the origin of both frames. (a) Find the barn-frame times at which the pole is fully inside, and choose the farmer's simultaneous door-shutting to be at the midpoint of that window. (b) Tabulate the four events AAA, BBB (nose reaches the exit door), FFF (entrance door shuts) and RRR (exit door shuts) in both frames. (c) In the runner's frame, show explicitly that neither door ever touches the pole.

Solution

(a) The window. γ=5/3\gamma=5/3γ=5/3, so the pole is contracted to 15/γ=9 m15/\gamma=9\ \mathrm{m}15/γ=9 m in the barn frame. At ct=0ct=0ct=0 the tail is at x=0x=0x=0 and the nose at x=9x=9x=9. The nose reaches x=10x=10x=10 after the pole advances 1 m1\ \mathrm{m}1 m, which takes ct=1/0.8=1.25 mct = 1/0.8 = 1.25\ \mathrm{m}ct=1/0.8=1.25 m. So the pole is wholly inside for 0<ct<1.25 m0 \lt ct \lt 1.25\ \mathrm{m}0<ct<1.25 m (that is, for 4.17 ns4.17\ \mathrm{ns}4.17 ns), and the farmer shuts both doors at ct=0.625 mct = 0.625\ \mathrm{m}ct=0.625 m.

(b) The table. Transform with ct′=γ(ct−βx)ct'=\gamma(ct-\beta x)ct′=γ(ct−βx), x′=γ(x−βct)x'=\gamma(x-\beta ct)x′=γ(x−βct) and γ=5/3\gamma=5/3γ=5/3, β=0.8\beta=0.8β=0.8:

Eventctctct (m)xxx (m)ct′ct'ct′ (m)x′x'x′ (m)
AAA   tail reaches entrance000000000000
BBB   nose reaches exit1.251.251.25101010−11.25-11.25−11.25151515
FFF   entrance door shuts0.6250.6250.625000+1.0417+1.0417+1.0417−0.8333-0.8333−0.8333
RRR   exit door shuts0.6250.6250.625101010−12.2917-12.2917−12.2917+15.8333+15.8333+15.8333

Read the fourth column. In the barn frame FFF and RRR are simultaneous. In the runner's frame RRR happens at ct′=−12.29ct'=-12.29ct′=−12.29 and FFF at ct′=+1.04ct'=+1.04ct′=+1.04 — the exit door shuts 13.33 m/c=44.5 ns13.33\ \mathrm{m}/c = 44.5\ \mathrm{ns}13.33 m/c=44.5 ns earlier, matching (2.2.56). Note also xB′=15 mx'_{B}=15\ \mathrm{m}xB′​=15 m, the pole's proper length ✓, and that in the runner's frame the nose reaches the exit at ct′=−11.25ct'=-11.25ct′=−11.25, i.e. well before the tail reaches the entrance at ct′=0ct'=0ct′=0. The pole is sticking out of both ends at once, which is what a 15 m15\ \mathrm{m}15 m pole does in a 6 m6\ \mathrm{m}6 m barn.

(c) Nobody gets hit. In the runner's frame the pole is at rest occupying 0≤x′≤150\leq x'\leq150≤x′≤15. Track the doors. The exit door is the worldline x=10x=10x=10; substituting ct=ct′/γ+β⋅10ct = ct'/\gamma + \beta\cdot 10ct=ct′/γ+β⋅10 into x′=γ(x−βct)x'=\gamma(x-\beta ct)x′=γ(x−βct) gives

xexit′(ct′)=γ(1−β2)10−β ct′=6−0.8 ct′. x'_{\text{exit}}(ct') = \gamma\big(1-\beta^{2}\big)10 - \beta\,ct' = 6 - 0.8\,ct'. xexit′​(ct′)=γ(1−β2)10−βct′=6−0.8ct′.

It reaches the nose, x′=15x'=15x′=15, when 6−0.8ct′=156-0.8ct'=156−0.8ct′=15, i.e. ct′=−11.25ct'=-11.25ct′=−11.25 ✓ (event BBB). It shuts at ct′=−12.29ct'=-12.29ct′=−12.29, which is earlier — at that moment it sits at x′=6+0.8(12.2917)=15.83 mx'=6+0.8(12.2917)=15.83\ \mathrm{m}x′=6+0.8(12.2917)=15.83 m, which is beyond the nose. The door shuts in empty space in front of the pole, reopens, and the pole then passes through.

The entrance door is x=0x=0x=0, worldline xent′(ct′)=−0.8 ct′x'_{\text{ent}}(ct')=-0.8\,ct'xent′​(ct′)=−0.8ct′. It shuts at ct′=+1.0417ct'=+1.0417ct′=+1.0417, when it sits at x′=−0.833 mx'=-0.833\ \mathrm{m}x′=−0.833 m — behind the tail, which is at x′=0x'=0x′=0. It too shuts in empty space.

The point. Every frame-independent question — did a door hit the pole? did the nose pass the exit before or after the exit door shut? — gets the same answer in both frames. Only "were the doors shut simultaneously?" differs, and that was never a fact about the world. If you insist on a barn that genuinely traps the pole, you must shut the doors and keep them shut, and then the runner's frame will report that the nose crumples against the closed exit door while the tail is still outside — a real, invariant, and rather expensive event that both frames agree on.

Problem 3 — two boosts in different directions leave a rotation behind

Work in the (ct,x,y)(ct,x,y)(ct,x,y) subspace. (a) Show that a pure boost matrix — in any direction — is symmetric. (b) Compute M=Λy(ϕ2)Λx(ϕ1)M=\Lambda_{y}(\phi_{2})\Lambda_{x}(\phi_{1})M=Λy​(ϕ2​)Λx​(ϕ1​) explicitly and show it is not symmetric unless one rapidity vanishes. Conclude that it cannot be a pure boost, so boosts do not form a group. (c) Show that the leftover is a rotation, and estimate its size for small rapidities. Quote (⚑) the exact angle and check your estimate against it.

Solution

(a) Pure boosts are symmetric. A boost along xxx is (2.2.48) padded with identity rows, manifestly symmetric. A boost in a general direction n^\hat nn^ is that one conjugated by a rotation RRR that takes n^\hat nn^ to x^\hat xx^: Λn^=RTΛxR\Lambda_{\hat n} = R^{\mathsf T}\Lambda_{x}RΛn^​=RTΛx​R (with RRR acting trivially on ctctct). Then Λn^T=RTΛxTR=RTΛxR=Λn^\Lambda_{\hat n}^{\mathsf T} = R^{\mathsf T}\Lambda_{x}^{\mathsf T}R = R^{\mathsf T}\Lambda_{x}R = \Lambda_{\hat n}Λn^T​=RTΛxT​R=RTΛx​R=Λn^​ ✓. So symmetry is the algebraic signature of "pure boost, no rotation".

(b) The product. With ci=cosh⁡ϕic_{i}=\cosh\phi_{i}ci​=coshϕi​, si=sinh⁡ϕis_{i}=\sinh\phi_{i}si​=sinhϕi​ and rows/columns ordered (ct,x,y)(ct,x,y)(ct,x,y):

Λx(ϕ1)=(c1−s10−s1c10001),Λy(ϕ2)=(c20−s2010−s20c2), \Lambda_{x}(\phi_{1}) = \begin{pmatrix} c_{1} & -s_{1} & 0\\ -s_{1} & c_{1} & 0\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Lambda_{y}(\phi_{2}) = \begin{pmatrix} c_{2} & 0 & -s_{2}\\ 0&1&0\\ -s_{2} & 0 & c_{2}\end{pmatrix}, Λx​(ϕ1​)=​c1​−s1​0​−s1​c1​0​001​​,Λy​(ϕ2​)=​c2​0−s2​​010​−s2​0c2​​​, M=Λy(ϕ2) Λx(ϕ1)=(c1c2−s1c2−s2−s1c10−s2c1s1s2c2). M = \Lambda_{y}(\phi_{2})\,\Lambda_{x}(\phi_{1}) = \begin{pmatrix} c_{1}c_{2} & -s_{1}c_{2} & -s_{2}\\ -s_{1} & c_{1} & 0\\ -s_{2}c_{1} & s_{1}s_{2} & c_{2}\end{pmatrix}. M=Λy​(ϕ2​)Λx​(ϕ1​)=​c1​c2​−s1​−s2​c1​​−s1​c2​c1​s1​s2​​−s2​0c2​​​.

Compare entries across the diagonal: M01=−s1c2M_{01}=-s_{1}c_{2}M01​=−s1​c2​ against M10=−s1M_{10}=-s_{1}M10​=−s1​; these agree only if c2=1c_{2}=1c2​=1, i.e. ϕ2=0\phi_{2}=0ϕ2​=0. Likewise M12=0M_{12}=0M12​=0 against M21=s1s2M_{21}=s_{1}s_{2}M21​=s1​s2​. So MMM is not symmetric, hence by (a) not a pure boost. Two boosts in different directions do not compose to a boost. The set of pure boosts is therefore not closed, and is not a group — only the boosts along a fixed axis are, which is what §3 actually proved.

(c) What is left over. ⚑ Every proper orthochronous Lorentz transformation factors uniquely as M=B RM = B\,RM=BR with BBB a pure boost and RRR a rotation (the polar decomposition; we quote it). Since MMM is not symmetric, R≠IR\neq IR=I: there is a residual rotation, the Wigner rotation, in the xyxyxy plane.

Its size for small rapidities follows from non-commutativity. Write Λx(ϕ)=exp⁡(ϕKx)\Lambda_{x}(\phi)=\exp(\phi K_{x})Λx​(ϕ)=exp(ϕKx​) and Λy(ϕ)=exp⁡(ϕKy)\Lambda_{y}(\phi)=\exp(\phi K_{y})Λy​(ϕ)=exp(ϕKy​) with generators

Kx=(0−10−100000),Ky=(00−1000−100). K_{x} = \begin{pmatrix}0&-1&0\\-1&0&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad K_{y}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&-1\\0&0&0\\-1&0&0\end{pmatrix}. Kx​=​0−10​−100​000​​,Ky​=​00−1​000​−100​​.

Multiplying out, [Ky,Kx]=KyKx−KxKy[K_{y},K_{x}] = K_{y}K_{x}-K_{x}K_{y}[Ky​,Kx​]=Ky​Kx​−Kx​Ky​ has entries only in the xyxyxy block:

[Ky,Kx]=(00000−1010)  ≡  Jz, [K_{y},K_{x}] = \begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\0&0&-1\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix} \;\equiv\; J_{z}, [Ky​,Kx​]=​000​001​0−10​​≡Jz​,

the generator of rotations about zzz. ⚑ By the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula (Chapter 6.1), eAeB=exp⁡ ⁣(A+B+12[A,B]+⋯)\ee^{A}\ee^{B}=\exp\!\big(A+B+\tfrac12[A,B]+\cdots\big)eAeB=exp(A+B+21​[A,B]+⋯), so

M=exp⁡ ⁣(ϕ2Ky+ϕ1Kx+12ϕ1ϕ2Jz+⋯), M = \exp\!\Big(\phi_{2}K_{y}+\phi_{1}K_{x} + \tfrac12\phi_{1}\phi_{2}J_{z}+\cdots\Big), M=exp(ϕ2​Ky​+ϕ1​Kx​+21​ϕ1​ϕ2​Jz​+⋯),

giving a rotation angle Ω≈12ϕ1ϕ2≈12β1β2\Omega\approx\tfrac12\phi_{1}\phi_{2}\approx\tfrac12\beta_{1}\beta_{2}Ω≈21​ϕ1​ϕ2​≈21​β1​β2​ at low speed. It is second order in the velocities, which is why it has no Newtonian counterpart and why nobody stumbled on it before 1926.

⚑ The exact angle, quoted, for two perpendicular boosts:

tan⁡Ω=γ1γ2 β1β2γ1+γ2. \tan\Omega = \frac{\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}\,\beta_{1}\beta_{2}}{\gamma_{1}+\gamma_{2}}. tanΩ=γ1​+γ2​γ1​γ2​β1​β2​​.

Check the low-speed limit: γi→1\gamma_{i}\to1γi​→1 and tan⁡Ω→Ω\tan\Omega\to\OmegatanΩ→Ω give Ω→β1β2/2\Omega\to\beta_{1}\beta_{2}/2Ω→β1​β2​/2 ✓, matching the commutator estimate. Numerically, for β1=β2=0.6\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=0.6β1​=β2​=0.6 the exact formula gives Ω=0.2213 rad=12.7∘\Omega=0.2213\ \mathrm{rad}=12.7^{\circ}Ω=0.2213 rad=12.7∘, and the two leading-order estimates bracket it — 12β1β2=0.1800\tfrac12\beta_{1}\beta_{2}=0.180021​β1​β2​=0.1800 from below and 12ϕ1ϕ2=0.2402\tfrac12\phi_{1}\phi_{2}=0.240221​ϕ1​ϕ2​=0.2402 from above, since β<ϕ\beta\lt\phiβ<ϕ for β>0\beta\gt0β>0. They are the same estimate to leading order and only differ at the next one: for β1=β2=0.01\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=0.01β1​=β2​=0.01 the exact angle is 5.00025×10−55.00025\times10^{-5}5.00025×10−5, against 5.00000×10−55.00000\times10^{-5}5.00000×10−5 and 5.00033×10−55.00033\times10^{-5}5.00033×10−5 — agreement to five figures.

Why it matters. An electron in an atom is continuously boosted in changing directions by the nuclear Coulomb field. The accumulated Wigner rotations make its spin precess — the Thomas precession — and this contributes a factor of 12\tfrac1221​ to the spin–orbit coupling in atomic fine structure. Without it, the predicted fine-structure splitting is wrong by a factor of two, and the discrepancy stood unexplained for two years. A pure kinematic effect, with no force involved at all, showing up in a spectrometer.

Problem 4 — a rocket at constant proper acceleration

A rocket accelerates so that its crew feel a constant aaa — that is, its acceleration measured in its own instantaneous rest frame is always aaa. (a) Show that its rapidity grows linearly in proper time, ϕ=aτ/c\phi = a\tau/cϕ=aτ/c, and hence β=tanh⁡(aτ/c)\beta=\tanh(a\tau/c)β=tanh(aτ/c). (b) Find the lab-frame time and distance as functions of τ\tauτ. (c) With a=g=9.81 m s−2a=g=9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}a=g=9.81 ms−2, compute β\betaβ, the lab time and the distance after 111 year of proper time, and then the proper time needed to reach the galactic centre, 26 00026\,00026000 light-years away. Comment.

Solution

(a) The rapidity grows linearly. This is where §6 pays for itself. In a proper-time interval dτ\dd\taudτ, the rocket's instantaneous rest frame sees it acquire a velocity dv=a dτ\dd v = a\,\dd\taudv=adτ, hence a rapidity increment

dϕ=artanh⁡ ⁣(a dτc)=a dτc+O ⁣(dτ3). \dd\phi = \operatorname{artanh}\!\left(\frac{a\,\dd\tau}{c}\right) = \frac{a\,\dd\tau}{c} + O\!\big(\dd\tau^{3}\big). dϕ=artanh(cadτ​)=cadτ​+O(dτ3).

Because rapidities add ((2.2.50)), these increments simply accumulate — no composition formula is needed, which is exactly what would have made the velocity version painful. Integrating from rest,

ϕ(τ)=aτc,β(τ)=tanh⁡ ⁣aτc,γ(τ)=cosh⁡ ⁣aτc. \phi(\tau) = \frac{a\tau}{c}, \qquad \beta(\tau) = \tanh\!\frac{a\tau}{c}, \qquad \gamma(\tau)=\cosh\!\frac{a\tau}{c}. ϕ(τ)=caτ​,β(τ)=tanhcaτ​,γ(τ)=coshcaτ​.

(b) Lab time and distance. By (2.2.31), dt=γ dτ=cosh⁡(aτ/c) dτ\dd t = \gamma\,\dd\tau = \cosh(a\tau/c)\,\dd\taudt=γdτ=cosh(aτ/c)dτ, so

t(τ)=casinh⁡ ⁣aτc. t(\tau) = \frac{c}{a}\sinh\!\frac{a\tau}{c}. t(τ)=ac​sinhcaτ​.

And dx=v dt=ctanh⁡(aτ/c)⋅cosh⁡(aτ/c) dτ=csinh⁡(aτ/c) dτ\dd x = v\,\dd t = c\tanh(a\tau/c)\cdot\cosh(a\tau/c)\,\dd\tau = c\sinh(a\tau/c)\,\dd\taudx=vdt=ctanh(aτ/c)⋅cosh(aτ/c)dτ=csinh(aτ/c)dτ, so

x(τ)=c2a[cosh⁡ ⁣aτc−1]. x(\tau) = \frac{c^{2}}{a}\left[\cosh\!\frac{a\tau}{c} - 1\right]. x(τ)=ac2​[coshcaτ​−1].

Eliminating τ\tauτ with cosh⁡2−sinh⁡2=1\cosh^{2}-\sinh^{2}=1cosh2−sinh2=1 gives (x+c2/a)2−c2t2=(c2/a)2\left(x+c^{2}/a\right)^{2}-c^{2}t^{2}=\left(c^{2}/a\right)^{2}(x+c2/a)2−c2t2=(c2/a)2: the worldline is a hyperbola. Chapter 2.3 will show that this is the spacetime analogue of a circle — the curve of constant "curvature" — and Chapter 3.1 will note that its crew experience something remarkably like a gravitational field, complete with a horizon behind them.

(c) Numbers. The natural scale is

cg=2.998×1089.81=3.06×107 s=0.969 yr,c2g=0.969 ly. \frac{c}{g} = \frac{2.998\times10^{8}}{9.81} = 3.06\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{s} = 0.969\ \mathrm{yr}, \qquad \frac{c^{2}}{g} = 0.969\ \mathrm{ly}. gc​=9.812.998×108​=3.06×107 s=0.969 yr,gc2​=0.969 ly.

A pleasant accident of our units: one year at one gee is very nearly one rapidity unit.

(Lab time: 26 00126\,00126001 years. The Galaxy does not get a discount.)

Comment. Two things are worth extracting. First, the crew never detect anything odd: their accelerometer reads a constant ggg forever, their rapidity climbs without limit at 1.031.031.03 per year, and at no point do they approach a barrier. It is only the velocity that saturates, and velocity is the badly chosen coordinate — this is (2.2.46) made visceral. Second, the crew-time cost of a journey grows only logarithmically with distance once you are relativistic, since ϕ≈ln⁡(2ax/c2)\phi\approx\ln(2ax/c^{2})ϕ≈ln(2ax/c2) for large xxx: the Andromeda galaxy, 2.52.52.5 million light-years away, costs 14.9714.9714.97 years of crew time against 10.5510.5510.55 for the galactic centre. The Universe is traversable within a lifetime and simultaneously unreachable, because you can never come home. Chapter 2.5 supplies the reason nobody does it: the fuel.

The brick you just laid

You derived (2.2.19) — ct′=γ(ct−βx)ct'=\gamma(ct-\beta x)ct′=γ(ct−βx), x′=γ(x−βct)x'=\gamma(x-\beta ct)x′=γ(x−βct), y′=yy'=yy′=y, z′=zz'=zz′=z — from the two postulates plus homogeneity, isotropy and reciprocity, with every step forced and every assumption named. You showed it reduces to Galileo as c→∞c\to\inftyc→∞, that boosts along an axis compose into boosts, that the composition is addition in rapidity and not in velocity, and that the quantity c2t2−x2−y2−z2c^{2}t^{2}-x^{2}-y^{2}-z^{2}c2t2−x2−y2−z2 is invariant even though you only ever demanded it for light. Simultaneity, dilation and contraction came out as corollaries in that order, and the two classical paradoxes turned out to be one paradox with two costumes.

Where this gets spent. Chapter 2.3 takes the invariant interval (2.2.21) and the hyperbolic form (2.2.48) and shows that together they define a geometry — spacetime, in which a boost is a rotation and proper time is arc length. Chapter 2.4 takes the matrix (2.2.24), calls it Λμν\Lambda^{\mu}{}_{\nu}Λμν​, and defines a tensor as anything that transforms with it — the rapidity form and the group property of §3 and §6 are quoted there verbatim. Chapter 2.5 applies the same transformation to momentum and energy instead of position and time, and E=mc2E=mc^{2}E=mc2 falls out of it; the γ\gammaγ you derived here is the γ\gammaγ in E=γmc2E=\gamma mc^{2}E=γmc2. Chapter 2.6 shows that the electric and magnetic fields transform into each other under exactly this boost, which retroactively explains Chapter 2.1's entire crisis. Chapter 3.1 keeps the transformation but only locally, which is the whole idea of general relativity. And Chapter 6.1 returns to the rapidity ϕ\phiϕ and names what it has been all along: the parameter of a one-parameter Lie group, with the boost generator KKK as its Lie-algebra element.
